title: IB ESS Exam Technique for the November Session
summary: IB ESS exam technique for November: master paper timing, command terms, data questions and essays with a focused three-week plan for SL and HL.
body_markdown:
Three weeks before the November session, the problem is rarely a complete lack of ESS knowledge. It is usually a gap between knowing something and turning it into marks under time pressure.


Effective **IB ESS exam technique** means reading evidence before interpreting it, matching the depth of an answer to its mark value, following command terms precisely, and leaving enough time for extended responses. Under the current ESS course, first assessed in 2026, SL and HL students both sit Paper 1 and Paper 2, but their timings and requirements differ.


Imagine an ESS student entering the final three weeks. Their notes are reasonably complete, but graphs still take too long and essays tend to become descriptive. The goal is not to relearn the course. It is to make good decisions repeatable.


### Your ESS exam checklist


Before building the plan, know what success looks like:


- Confirm whether you are sitting SL or HL and learn your exact paper timings.
- Practise extracting evidence from unfamiliar sources.
- Match each response to the command term and available marks.
- Show calculations, units and intermediate steps.
- Prepare adaptable real-world examples rather than memorised essays.
- Complete timed practice in Exam mode and review every lost mark.
- Check the official schedule for your examination zone.


The current IB ESS course combines scientific and social perspectives, so strong answers must often connect environmental processes, stakeholders, values and management strategies. RevisionDojo’s[new-syllabus ESS resource hub](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-environmental-systems-and-societies-ess-new-syllabus) keeps Study Notes, Flashcards and exam-style practice together for that purpose.


### Know the current ESS paper structure


The current IB subject brief confirms that ESS is available at both SL and HL from first assessment in 2026. Paper 1 uses a previously unseen case study. Paper 2 combines short-answer and data-based work with structured essays.


Component SL HL


Paper 1 1 hour, 35 marks, 25% 2 hours, 70 marks, 30%


Paper 2 2 hours, 60 marks, 50% 2 hours 30 minutes, 80 marks, 50%


Paper 2 Section A 40 marks 40 marks


Paper 2 Section B One 20-mark structured essay from a choice of two Two 20-mark structured essays from a choice of three


The remaining weighting comes from the individual investigation: 25% at SL and 20% at HL. This matters psychologically. Your examination performance is important, but no single awkward question determines the entire result.


For session logistics, use the[RevisionDojo November ESS exam dates guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-ess-november-2026-exam-dates) alongside the official schedule supplied by your school. Examination dates and local start arrangements should always be confirmed with your coordinator.


### Three weeks out: turn content into Paper 1 marks


In the first week, our hypothetical student stops rereading whole chapters. Instead, they open the[ESS Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-environmental-systems-and-societies-ess-new-syllabus/questionbank) and work through unfamiliar graphs, maps, tables and case-study extracts.


Paper 1 rewards disciplined reading. Begin with the question, identify the command term, note the marks, and then locate the relevant source. Do not explain every visible feature of a graph when the question asks for one trend.


Use these techniques:


- **State or identify:** give the requested fact directly. A one-mark response normally does not need a paragraph.
- **Describe:** report what the source shows, including direction, magnitude or comparison where relevant.
- **Calculate:** write the formula or method, substitute values, show working and include units when applicable.
- **Explain:** connect cause and effect. Words such as “because,” “therefore” and “leading to” help expose the reasoning.
- **Analyse:** select patterns or relationships, support them with source evidence, and explain their significance.
- **Evaluate:** consider strengths and limitations, competing perspectives or consequences, then reach a supported judgment.


When citing data, be specific. “Pollution increased” is weaker than identifying the relevant period and quantifying the change correctly. Also check axes, scales, legends and units before calculating. A graph can be read accurately but interpreted wrongly because the student overlooked a logarithmic scale or confused percentage change with percentage-point change.


Allocate Paper 1 time broadly in proportion to marks while reserving a few minutes for checks. SL students have about 1.7 minutes per mark; HL students have roughly the same average. That is a planning guide, not an instruction to abandon a nearly complete response when a stopwatch beeps.


A student negotiates with an hourglass full of tiny examiners while trying not to check the clock


### Two weeks out: build a controlled Paper 2 method


By the second week, the student’s attention shifts to Paper 2. Section A demands accurate knowledge, application and data handling. Section B tests whether that knowledge can be organised into an argument.


For short responses, let the marks shape the answer. A two-mark “outline” needs two clear pieces of relevant information or sufficient development for the available credit. A four-mark “explain” usually requires more than four disconnected facts. It needs developed causal reasoning.


If a question gives a scenario, use it. Generic textbook knowledge may be correct yet fail to answer the specific problem. Name the ecosystem, stakeholder, policy or data pattern provided, then apply ESS concepts to it.


For essay choice, spend a brief moment comparing every option. Choose the question for which you can produce:


- accurate subject knowledge;
- relevant real-world examples;
- more than one perspective;
- a clear line of argument;
- a justified conclusion.


Each 20-mark structured essay culminates in a nine-mark extended response assessed through markbands. Strong answers use accurate ESS terminology, develop ideas rather than listing them, integrate examples, consider different viewpoints and answer the exact question. At HL, responses should also draw meaningfully on relevant HL understanding and lenses, including environmental law, environmental economics and environmental ethics where appropriate.


A useful plan is claim, evidence or example, analysis, alternative perspective, and judgment. Do not force every paragraph into an identical template, but make each paragraph advance the argument. The[guide to ethics in HL ESS questions](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-do-ethics-fit-into-ess-hl-exam-questions-2026-first-assessment) can help HL students move beyond merely naming an ethical position.


### The final week: practise decisions under time pressure


The final week should feel narrower, not busier. Our student now completes one timed Paper 1 and one timed Paper 2 in Exam mode. The purpose is to rehearse pacing, question selection and recovery when an answer feels uncertain.


After each attempt, classify mistakes:


- **Knowledge gap:** revisit the relevant Study Notes and use Flashcards for retrieval.
- **Command-term error:** rewrite the response at the required depth.
- **Evidence error:** practise quoting or calculating from the source.
- **Timing error:** set checkpoints for the next simulation.
- **Essay structure error:** produce a fresh plan before rewriting selected paragraphs.


Revision is most useful when feedback changes the next attempt. RevisionDojo’s Grading tools and AI Chat can help diagnose unclear reasoning, while Mock Exams and Predicted Papers provide longer practice. The[ESS exam mistakes guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-are-the-biggest-mistakes-students-make-in-ess-exams-2026-first-assessment) is useful for checking whether the same weakness keeps returning.


Avoid filling every remaining hour. A[realistic final week before IB exams](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/realistic-final-week-before-exams) protects sleep, recall and concentration. The night before each paper, review compact examples, command terms and logistics rather than attempting to master an untouched topic.


### What to do when a question feels unfamiliar


ESS questions often feel unfamiliar because they place familiar concepts inside a new environmental context. Pause and separate the source from the syllabus concept.


First, underline the command term and subject of the question. Next, identify any relevant system, process, stakeholder or perspective. Then use the supplied evidence and connect it to what you know. If uncertain, write the most defensible answer you can and move on. Leaving a response blank removes every possibility of earning partial credit.


The calm student is not necessarily the one who knows everything. It is the one who has rehearsed what to do when knowledge is incomplete.


### Make the final three weeks count


The November session rewards more than memory. It rewards selection: the right evidence, the right depth, the right example and the right amount of time.


Use RevisionDojo as the centre of that final process. Target weaknesses in the Questionbank, refresh ideas through Study Notes and Flashcards, ask AI Chat to clarify difficult links, and use Grading tools to improve written reasoning. Then sit timed papers in Exam mode so exam technique becomes behaviour rather than intention.


Three weeks is not enough time to make every answer perfect. It is enough time to make your method dependable.
